prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- As familiar and reassuring as the map of the world is, there is only so much that physical geography can tell us about the state of the planet. Forest loss: This cartogram shows areas where the worst deforestation occured from 1990 to 2000. A new book, The Atlas of the Real World, has redrawn the map giving vivid new insights and bringing economic, social and environmental data to life. Not since the German meteorologist, Alfred Wegener, sketched out the first detailed theories of continental drift has the world appeared so misshapen, so otherworldly. The 366 cartograms (statistical maps) which make up the book twist, shrink and distend countries and continents into all sorts of shapes and sizes. The book and the accompanying Web site were devised by Daniel Dorling, professor of human geography at the UK's University of Sheffield, Anna Barford, a research associate at Sheffield and Mark Newman, a professor of physics at the University of Michigan. Work on the project began in earnest in 2006 when Dorling teamed up with Newman, who had co-created a new software technique for creating equal area cartograms the year before. With the software in place, the painstaking task of assembling the data began. The information was drawn from a variety of organizations including the United Nations, the World Health Organization and the World Bank. For ease of visual comparison, territories are split into 12 geographical regions -- e.g. blue for North America, brown for Northern Africa -- and shading marks out specific countries. The range of subjects is impressive, from greenhouse gas emissions, wealth and disease to more obscure data about numbers of dentists and working tractors. John Pritchard, research assistant at University of Sheffield and part of the team working on the project, told CNN: "I think the maps of disease are particularly shocking and bring home the scale of the problem in Africa better than a table of statistics does." Indeed, the map of malaria deaths is striking: 94 percent of deaths from malaria occur in Africa, making the continent appear like a vast bloated blob. The rest of the world is reduced to a disparate series of veiny streaks. There are other sobering statistics to consider. In June 2008, Principal Voices spoke to Head of Research at Oxfam GB Duncan Green about strategies to eradicate poverty. Green talked about the education being crucial to breaking the cycle of poverty, particularly for girls. The new atlas's Girls not at Primary School cartogram graphically illustrates the lack of female education in many parts of the developing world. Team members are currently working on a map of languages and soon hope to be producing animated maps. "We have a series of maps that show deaths at various stages, which would be particularly suited to an animation, and we now have a PhD student looking at extending the Web site, including ways of mapping flow." Pritchard said.

LONDON, England (CNN) — Although the traditional world map may look recognizable and comforting, physical geography alone reveals only a limited picture of the planet’s condition.

One cartogram on forest loss highlights the places that experienced the most severe deforestation between 1990 and 2000. It appears in a new book, *The Atlas of the Real World*, which reshapes the global map to present economic, social and environmental information in a vivid and revealing way.

The world has rarely looked so distorted and unfamiliar—not since German meteorologist Alfred Wegener first outlined detailed theories of continental drift. The book contains 366 cartograms, or statistical maps, that enlarge, compress and contort nations and continents into widely varying forms and proportions.

The book and its companion website were created by Daniel Dorling, a professor of human geography at the University of Sheffield in the United Kingdom; Anna Barford, a Sheffield research associate; and Mark Newman, a physics professor at the University of Michigan.

The project began in earnest in 2006, when Dorling joined forces with Newman. A year earlier, Newman had helped develop a new software method for producing equal-area cartograms. Once that technology was available, the team began the labor-intensive process of gathering the necessary statistics.

Their data came from numerous institutions, including the United Nations, the World Health Organization and the World Bank. To make visual comparisons easier, territories are organized into 12 geographic regions. North America, for example, is shown in blue, while Northern Africa is brown; different shades distinguish individual countries.

The atlas covers an extensive range of topics, including greenhouse-gas emissions, wealth and disease, as well as less commonly mapped statistics such as the number of dentists and tractors in use.

John Pritchard, a University of Sheffield research assistant and member of the project team, told CNN that the disease maps were especially startling and conveyed the magnitude of Africa’s difficulties more effectively than a statistical table.

The cartogram of malaria deaths is particularly dramatic. Africa accounts for 94 percent of all malaria fatalities, causing the continent to swell into an enormous, inflated mass, while the rest of the world contracts into scattered, vein-like lines.

Other figures are equally troubling. In June 2008, *Principal Voices* interviewed Duncan Green, Oxfam GB’s head of research, about approaches to eliminating poverty. Green emphasized that education—especially for girls—is essential to ending the poverty cycle. The atlas’s cartogram titled “Girls Not at Primary School” provides a powerful visual representation of the shortage of educational opportunities for girls across many areas of the developing world.

The team is now developing a map of languages and hopes soon to create animated cartograms. Pritchard said that a sequence of maps depicting deaths at different stages would work particularly well as an animation. He added that a PhD student was exploring ways to expand the website, including methods for mapping flows.

Created by geographers Daniel Dorling, Mark Newman, and Anna Barford, it contains 366 computer-generated cartograms in which countries and regions are resized according to statistical data rather than their physical land area. Drawing on information from international organizations, the atlas maps a broad range of economic, social, demographic, health, and environmental indicators.

In each cartogram, the size of a territory reflects its share of the subject being measured. Countries may therefore expand dramatically, shrink almost to invisibility, or assume unfamiliar shapes. A nation with a large population, a powerful economy, or high energy consumption becomes proportionally larger on the relevant map, while one with a small share of that measure contracts. This method transforms abstract figures into images that can be grasped quickly and compared across regions.

The resulting distortions reveal patterns that conventional maps often conceal. Maps of wealth, trade, resource use, and carbon emissions emphasize the dominance of industrialized countries, while those showing poverty, malnutrition, infectious disease, and preventable deaths enlarge other parts of the world. Africa is particularly striking: although it may appear small on maps of income or consumption, it expands dramatically when the atlas represents conditions such as malaria, HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and inadequate access to health care.

These contrasts make global inequality visible in an immediate and memorable way. Instead of asking readers to interpret long tables of numbers, the atlas allows them to see where resources, opportunities, risks, and suffering are concentrated. By reshaping the world according to lived realities rather than geographical area, *The Atlas of the Real World* turns complex international statistics into a powerful visual account of how unevenly the world’s wealth, health, and environmental burdens are distributed.

counterfactuals.output:
# When the world is reshaped by data, inequality comes into focus

**By CNN-style feature staff**

**Cambridge, England** — On a conventional world map, countries are defined by their physical size. Russia stretches across Eurasia, Canada dominates the north and small island nations can be difficult to find.

But in *The Atlas of the Real World*, geography is not fixed.

The book, created by geographer Daniel Dorling, physicist Mark Newman and researcher Anna Barford, uses cartograms — maps that enlarge or shrink territories according to a particular statistic — to show how wealth, population, disease, pollution and other forces are distributed across the planet.

The result is a world that can look startlingly unfamiliar. A country may swell dramatically on a map of economic output, nearly disappear when land area is replaced by population, or expand again when the subject turns to carbon emissions, infectious disease or access to basic services.

## Maps that put numbers in their place

A cartogram begins with recognizable national borders, but adjusts the area of each country to represent data rather than square miles. On a population map, for example, densely populated countries become much larger, while vast but sparsely inhabited regions contract.

That simple change gives statistics a geographic form.

Economic maps can show where global wealth, trade and consumption are concentrated. The United States, Western Europe and parts of East Asia often loom large when the measurement is income, spending or financial power. Poorer regions may shrink, even when they are home to substantial populations.

Social indicators reveal a different world. Maps tracking education, migration, internet access or employment can expose divides both between and within regions. Countries that appear prominent on a population cartogram may become far smaller when the map is redrawn according to university enrollment, research activity or access to technology.

## A distorted world that reveals reality

The visual distortions are intentional. Traditional maps can give physical territory more importance than the people and activities within it. Cartograms reverse that emphasis, turning abstract tables into images that can be understood at a glance.

Health data can produce some of the atlas’s most dramatic contrasts. Nations may expand according to rates of infectious disease, infant mortality or preventable deaths, while those with stronger health systems recede. Other maps, focused on medical spending or the availability of doctors, shift the visual weight back toward wealthier countries.

Placed side by side, the maps highlight a central global imbalance: The regions carrying the greatest burden of disease are not always those with the most health resources.

Environmental cartograms offer another perspective. A map based on carbon dioxide emissions can enlarge industrialized and rapidly developing economies, while low-emitting countries become thin slivers. Maps of resource use, energy consumption, waste or environmental risk show how responsibility for ecological damage may be concentrated far from the communities most vulnerable to its effects.

## More than a collection of statistics

First published in 2008, *The Atlas of the Real World* organizes hundreds of cartograms around major themes, including population, wealth, trade, health, education, conflict and the environment.

Its power comes from comparison. A nation’s shape changes from page to page, depending on what is being measured. The reader is encouraged to ask not only where people live, but where money is held, where resources are consumed, where emissions are produced and where hardship is concentrated.

The maps do have limitations. National averages can conceal sharp inequalities inside countries, and a cartogram’s warped borders can make precise locations harder to recognize. The images also reflect the quality and date of the underlying data.

Still, the atlas demonstrates why data visualization can be so effective. A spreadsheet may show that wealth and disease are unevenly distributed. A cartogram makes that imbalance physically visible.

In these maps, the world is never just one shape. It expands and contracts with each new measure — revealing a planet defined as much by inequality, movement and consumption as by mountains, oceans and borders.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on Daniel Dorling, Anna Barford, and Mark Newman’s project to redraw the world according to statistics, including examples involving deforestation, malaria deaths, and girls’ access to primary education.
counterfactuals.output:
## Worldmapper: redrawing the world by statistics

Geographer **Daniel Dorling** and researcher **Anna Barford**, then at the University of Sheffield, worked with physicist and network scientist **Mark Newman** of the University of Michigan to create **Worldmapper**, an online collection of statistical world maps launched in the mid-2000s.

Instead of giving each country its conventional land area, Worldmapper uses **cartograms**: countries expand or contract according to the quantity being mapped. Their approximate location is retained, so the map remains recognizable, but familiar geography is deliberately distorted. Newman helped develop the computer methods used to produce these area cartograms, while Dorling, Barford, and their collaborators assembled and interpreted international datasets.

The aim was to make global inequalities immediately visible. A table may show that a problem is concentrated in a few countries; a cartogram makes those countries physically dominate the world.

### Deforestation

On a map scaled by **forest loss**, countries experiencing extensive deforestation become disproportionately large. **Brazil**, because of forest clearance in the Amazon, is one of the most conspicuous territories. **Indonesia** and parts of tropical Africa and Latin America also expand, while countries with little forest or little recorded loss nearly disappear.

The image differs sharply from an ordinary map of forest cover. It does not simply show where forests exist; it emphasizes where forest area was being removed during the period covered by the underlying data—generally late-20th-century or early-2000s international statistics. The map therefore highlights the concentration of global forest depletion in tropical regions and the role of logging, agricultural expansion, ranching, and plantation development.

### Deaths from malaria

The cartogram of **malaria deaths** transforms the world even more dramatically. **Sub-Saharan Africa swells to dominate the map**, reflecting the overwhelming concentration of malaria mortality there, particularly among young children. Countries in Europe and much of North America virtually vanish, despite occupying large areas on a conventional map, because locally acquired malaria deaths are rare.

Parts of South and Southeast Asia remain visible, but the map’s central message is the extreme African burden. It also exposes the mismatch between disease impact and global wealth: the places enlarged by malaria mortality are generally among those with the fewest medical, public-health, and financial resources.

### Girls without access to primary education

For the map of **primary-school-age girls not enrolled in school**, land area and national wealth again become almost irrelevant. Countries with large populations and substantial barriers to girls’ schooling—especially **India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Ethiopia**, and other parts of South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa—expand considerably. Wealthier countries, where nearly all girls enter primary education, shrink to thin outlines or disappear.

This cartogram combines two factors: the proportion of girls excluded from school and the size of the relevant child population. Thus, a populous country with a moderate non-enrolment rate can appear larger than a smaller country with a worse percentage. The map is therefore best read as showing the **number of affected girls**, not simply the probability that an individual girl will be excluded.

## Significance and limitations

Worldmapper’s strength is rhetorical as well as analytical. By preserving recognizable national positions while changing their size, it challenges the conventional political map, in which large but sparsely populated territories appear more important than small, densely populated ones. Its maps reveal that the “shape of the world” changes depending on whether the subject is land, population, wealth, disease, environmental damage, or educational opportunity.

The maps do, however, depend on the quality and date of international data. Definitions of forest loss, malaria mortality, or school enrolment can vary, and missing or uncertain national statistics affect the resulting shapes. Cartograms can also make small countries difficult to identify and should be read alongside legends, tables, and notes.

Taken together, the deforestation, malaria, and girls’ education maps demonstrate the project’s core argument: **geographical size is only one way of depicting the world, and often not the most revealing one**.

counterfactuals.output:
# A World Remade by Numbers

On a conventional atlas, Russia sprawls across northern Eurasia, Greenland looms over the Atlantic and Africa often appears smaller than it really is. Equal-area cartograms replace that familiar geography with a more unsettling measure of the world: countries expand or contract according to population, wealth, disease, migration, carbon emissions or another chosen statistic.

The result is a map that behaves like an argument.

On a population cartogram, India and China balloon while sparsely inhabited countries recede. Map national income and North America, Western Europe and Japan swell dramatically. Map malaria deaths, maternal mortality or lack of access to basic services, and parts of Africa and South Asia grow to dominate the page. Borders remain recognizable where possible, but physical size no longer determines visual importance: equal quantities of the mapped variable are represented by equal areas.

Researchers associated with the University of Sheffield helped popularize this approach through the **Worldmapper** project. The team—whose work included geographer Danny Dorling and colleagues such as Anna Barford and Mark Newman—developed hundreds of cartograms designed to make global statistics immediately visible. Rather than asking readers to compare long columns of figures, the maps turn imbalance into shape.

Their raw material came from major international datasets, particularly those compiled by the **United Nations and its agencies**, as well as organizations such as the **World Bank** and the **World Health Organization**. Census returns, development indicators, health records, trade figures and environmental statistics were converted into territorial areas. Because the quality and date of reporting vary between countries, the maps are not presented as perfect snapshots; they are visual summaries of the best comparable data available.

A consistent color system helps viewers navigate the distortion. Countries are grouped into broad world regions—twelve in the project’s standard scheme—with each region assigned a distinctive color or family of shades. A country may become almost unrecognizably thin or enormously inflated, but its color and approximate position still identify the continent and regional group to which it belongs. The palette remains consistent from map to map, allowing readers to move quickly between subjects without relearning the visual language.

The power of these cartograms lies in the tension between familiarity and disruption. Coastlines bend, continents bulge and neighboring states are squeezed aside, yet the world remains just recognizable enough to compare with the mental map most people carry. That moment of recognition makes inequality difficult to ignore. A tiny state can become a giant when mapped by refugees, military spending or disease burden; a geographically vast country can nearly disappear when the subject is internet access, research output or private wealth.

The Sheffield team also envisaged moving beyond static images by creating **animated cartograms**. Such maps could show countries swelling and shrinking over time as populations shift, epidemics spread, economies rise or emissions accumulate. Animation would add a historical dimension to the project, turning a single distorted world into a sequence of changing global relationships.

Equal-area cartograms do not replace conventional maps, nor do they explain why inequalities exist. What they do is change the question. Instead of asking where countries are and how much land they occupy, they ask how much of a global phenomenon belongs to each place. In that transformed geography, statistics acquire borders—and inequality becomes something the eye can see.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how the 366 statistical maps in *The Atlas of the Real World* bring data to life, using quotations from research assistant John Pritchard and discussing the atlas’s most striking disease and poverty maps.
counterfactuals.output:
*The Atlas of the Real World* turns abstract statistics into images by redrawing the world 366 times—one map for every day of a leap year. Instead of keeping countries at their ordinary geographic size, each cartogram enlarges or shrinks them according to the quantity being measured, while preserving enough of their position and outline for the world to remain recognizable. As research assistant John Pritchard explained, the maps are “visually very powerful” and “speak for themselves”: “You don’t have to be a statistician to understand them.”

That visual method gives human consequences to numbers that otherwise seem remote. On maps of HIV/AIDS, malaria and other preventable diseases, sub-Saharan Africa expands grotesquely, while Europe and North America almost disappear. The distortion makes the unequal geography of illness impossible to overlook. HIV prevalence produces an especially shocking image, with southern African countries swollen far beyond their familiar proportions. Malaria deaths similarly inflate tropical Africa, showing that the burden falls overwhelmingly on populations with the fewest medical and economic resources. Maps of tuberculosis, maternal mortality and deaths in childbirth reinforce the same pattern: where health systems are weakest, countries become largest.

The poverty maps are equally striking. When territory represents the number of people living on very low incomes, India, China and parts of Africa balloon, while the richer countries of the global North contract. By contrast, maps of wealth, consumption and health expenditure reverse the picture: the United States, western Europe and Japan become dominant. Placed beside one another, these maps reveal that poverty is not simply the absence of money. It is closely connected to malnutrition, unsafe water, early death and vulnerability to treatable disease.

Pritchard’s observation that “you can see immediately where the inequalities are” captures the atlas’s central achievement. Its maps do not merely decorate tables of figures; they reorganize familiar space so that the statistic becomes the geography. Continents that usually dominate conventional atlases may nearly vanish, while places often pushed to the margins fill the page. The resulting distortions bring data to life by making inequality visible, comparative and emotionally difficult to ignore.

# New atlas redraws the world according to wealth, pollution, disease and opportunity

**LONDON —** In a new atlas, the familiar outline of the world bends, bulges and nearly disappears as countries are resized according to what they produce, consume, suffer or lack.

Instead of giving every nation the amount of space dictated by its physical area, *The Atlas of the Real World: Mapping the Way We Live* presents hundreds of cartograms in which territory expands or contracts according to data. On one map, countries are scaled by greenhouse gas emissions; on another, by wealth. Other maps show the distribution of dentists, tractors, forest loss, malaria deaths and female education.

The result is a planet that changes shape from page to page—and often bears little resemblance to the one displayed in classrooms.

Large polluters swell dramatically on maps of carbon emissions, while many poorer countries narrow to slivers. The pattern shifts on maps of malaria mortality, where parts of sub-Saharan Africa dominate and much of the industrialized world all but vanishes. Maps of wealth emphasize North America, Western Europe and parts of East Asia; maps of preventable disease show a profoundly different geography.

Created by geographer Daniel Dorling, statistician Anna Barford and physicist Mark Newman, the atlas is based on the Worldmapper project, which uses statistical cartograms to make global inequalities visually immediate. Its 366 maps—one for each day of a leap year—cover population, migration, transport, food, energy, health, education, employment, violence, trade and environmental change.

A conventional political map tells viewers where countries are and how much land they occupy. The new atlas asks a different question: How large would those countries appear if size reflected their share of a particular global phenomenon?

That method produces striking distortions. Countries with large populations often remain prominent across many subjects, but others change sharply depending on the measure. Japan and Western European nations may grow on maps of income, medical provision or long life expectancy, then shrink on maps of tropical disease. India and China loom large in measures influenced by population, though their relative size changes when the data are calculated around consumption, infrastructure or historical emissions.

The maps preserve broad geographic relationships, so neighboring countries generally remain connected, but their areas are altered in proportion to the selected statistic. Coastlines stretch, borders curve and continents become almost unrecognizable. Consistent colors help readers locate regions even when their familiar shapes have been transformed.

## A world inflated by carbon

The greenhouse gas maps provide some of the atlas’s clearest examples of uneven responsibility.

Industrialized countries and rapidly growing economies expand when the world is redrawn according to emissions. The United States becomes especially prominent in maps reflecting high levels of consumption and fossil-fuel use. Europe, China, Japan and other major economies also take up far more space than their physical geography would warrant.

Much of Africa, by contrast, becomes extremely small on maps of emissions, even though the continent is highly exposed to drought, changing rainfall, crop disruption and other effects associated with climate change.

The contrast illustrates one of the atlas’s central themes: the people most responsible for a global problem are not always those most vulnerable to its consequences.

Forest-loss maps tell a related but different story. Tropical countries can expand as land is cleared for agriculture, timber, mining or settlement. These images move attention away from the smokestacks and highways of industrial economies and toward the forests of Latin America, Africa and Southeast Asia. At the same time, they raise questions about international demand, because commodities linked to deforestation are frequently consumed far from where the trees are cut.

## Wealth reshapes the Northern Hemisphere

When countries are resized by income or wealth, the global map becomes heavily weighted toward North America, Europe and parts of East Asia. Regions with relatively small populations can appear enormous because of their share of global economic resources.

Poorer countries, including some with millions of residents, contract severely.

Placed beside maps of poverty, undernourishment or infectious disease, the wealth cartograms expose a mismatch between resources and need. Places with the greatest medical burdens often have the smallest shares of global income, health spending and specialized care.

That disparity becomes particularly vivid in the atlas’s maps of dentists and other health professionals. Wealthier countries balloon because they contain large numbers of trained practitioners and can support extensive systems of routine and preventive care. Many low-income countries shrink despite having substantial populations.

Dentists may seem like an eccentric measure of development, but their distribution reflects broader conditions: household income, professional education, public-health investment, urban infrastructure and access to regular treatment. A map of dentists therefore becomes an indirect map of institutional capacity.

## Tractors reveal the machinery of food production

The atlas also turns ordinary objects into indicators of global inequality.

On the map showing agricultural tractors, highly mechanized farming regions expand. Countries where farmers rely more heavily on manual labor or animal power contract. The image does not simply show where food is grown; it shows how farming is organized and how unevenly agricultural technology is distributed.

A large number of tractors can indicate capital-intensive agriculture and high labor productivity, although it does not necessarily mean that a country has more fertile land or a more sustainable food system. Mechanization can raise output, but it may also accompany heavy fuel use, soil compaction and dependence on industrial inputs.

By placing tractor ownership alongside maps of farm employment, food production and hunger, the atlas allows readers to see that agricultural abundance and food security are not determined by land area alone. Technology, purchasing power, trade and political stability also influence who has enough to eat.

## Malaria makes Africa loom

Few cartograms are as stark as those depicting malaria.

On a conventional map, Africa occupies a familiar share of the globe. On a map weighted by malaria deaths, the most heavily affected parts of the continent swell dramatically. Countries in Europe and North America become nearly invisible because locally acquired malaria deaths are rare there.

The distortion communicates the concentration of the disease more quickly than a table of mortality figures. It also shows how climate, poverty, housing, mosquito control, drug access and public-health systems combine to create radically different risks.

Yet the atlas’s editors caution through their presentation that maps of disease should not be read as maps of blame or as fixed portraits of national character. Health statistics are shaped by the quality of surveillance and reporting. Countries with weak institutions may undercount illness and deaths, meaning that some burdens are likely greater than the available figures suggest.

## Female education changes the map again

Maps of women’s and girls’ education offer another view of unequal opportunity.

Countries with broad access to schooling for girls expand when the map measures female enrollment or educational attainment. Those where girls are excluded from classrooms, leave school early or face shortages of teachers and facilities shrink on those measures—or grow when the variable is the number denied an education.

The distinction is important. Every cartogram depends on exactly what is being counted. A large country on a map of girls out of school represents deprivation, not success; a large country on a map of women completing education indicates wider access or, in some cases, a very large population.

Female education is closely connected to income, health and political participation. Higher levels of schooling for women are generally associated with lower maternal and infant mortality, improved family health and greater economic independence. By showing these subjects on adjacent pages, the atlas encourages readers to look for relationships rather than treat each statistic in isolation.

## Powerful images, but not conventional maps

Cartograms have limitations. A nation may dominate a page because it has a huge population, not because an individual resident is especially likely to experience the condition being mapped. Total greenhouse gas emissions, for example, answer a different question from emissions per person. Total wealth differs from average income, and the number of dentists differs from the number available per 100,000 residents.

The underlying data may also come from different years and from international agencies with varying methods. Definitions of disease, employment, schooling and forest loss are not always perfectly consistent across borders.

For those reasons, the atlas includes explanatory material and numerical context. The cartograms are intended as analytical tools rather than precise navigational maps. Their strength is not in showing exact borders but in making proportions visible.

That visual approach can produce an emotional response that conventional statistics rarely achieve. A reader may already know that malaria deaths are concentrated in poor tropical countries or that greenhouse gas emissions are disproportionately generated by wealthy economies. Seeing the world physically contorted by those facts gives the information new force.

Across its hundreds of maps, the atlas presents no single “real” shape of the planet. Instead, it argues that the world looks different depending on what is valued and counted.

Land area produces the map people know. Wealth, disease, machinery, education and pollution produce maps of the world they live in.
